title: Type erasure and reified type parameters
goal: By the end you can say what the JVM erases and what survives, predict where an unchecked cast really fails, write `inline` functions with `reified` type parameters for `is T`, `as? T` and `T::class`, and give Java callers a `Class<T>` version they can actually call.
opening:
Every box that comes into the storeroom passes the clerk at the door. The clerk reads its label, "Box of apples", checks that only apples go in, and nods it through. Then, as lesson 1 warned, the clerk tears the label off. On the shelves, a box of apples and a box of lemons look exactly alike, which is fine until someone wants a lemon.

Usually nobody minds: whoever opens a box was told at the door what it holds. The trouble starts when someone asks a box "are you a box of apples?" There's no label left to read.

In code, that question is `is List<Int>`, and the compiler refuses it. Worse, a cast to `List<String>` succeeds on a list of numbers, and the failure turns up later, somewhere else. The cast looks like a check, which makes it an easy trap.

Star projection: when you don't know the type ended at that refusal. In this lesson, we'll watch the label come off, then meet a clerk who copies it onto a note first. We'll see how Java passes the label by hand, and what the note can't hold. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: `val lies = listOf(180, 150) as Any as List<String>` compiles with a warning. What does `println(lies.size)` do?
options: It throws `ClassCastException` at the cast, before `println` runs
It prints `2`
It prints `0`, because no element is a String
It doesn't compile: Kotlin forbids casting to `List<String>`
warmup.why: At run time the list is just a `List`, so the cast can only check that it is a list, and it is. `size` never touches an element, so it prints `2`. The `ClassCastException` comes later, at the first read that needs a `String`. That delayed failure is what erasure costs you.

sections.h: The label comes off after the check: type erasure
sections.body:
The last lesson hit a wall: `is List<Int>` doesn't compile. Here is why. Both compilers check type arguments, and then remove them. At run time, a list of variety names and a list of weights are the same kind of object:

```java
List<String> varieties = new ArrayList<>();
List<Integer> weights = new ArrayList<>();
System.out.println(varieties.getClass() == weights.getClass());   // true: both are java.util.ArrayList
```

```kotlin
val varieties = ArrayList<String>()
val weights = ArrayList<Int>()
println(varieties.javaClass == weights.javaClass)                  // true: both are java.util.ArrayList
```

This is **type erasure**: the compiler checks each type argument, then leaves it out of the compiled code, so objects carry no record of it. It's the torn-off label. Kotlin compiles to the same JVM as Java and inherits the rule, so in both languages the `ArrayList` object has no field that says `String`.

Here is what both compilers leave in the class file. Each type parameter becomes its bound: a plain `T` becomes `Object`, and `T : Comparable<T>` becomes `Comparable`. So `List.get` returns an `Object`. Where your code needs a `String`, the compiler inserts a **`checkcast`** right after the call: a bytecode instruction that checks the object's class at run time, and throws `ClassCastException` if it's wrong. Run `javap -c`, the JDK tool that prints a class file's instructions, on any class that reads from a `List<String>`, and you'll see one. That inserted cast is the line that throws in the last example below.

Three things follow, and each has an error you'll meet:

- A type check can test only the class. `x is List<String>` fails with `cannot check for instance of erased type 'List<String>'.`, and `is T` fails the same way. Java says `Object cannot be safely cast to List<String>`.
- You can't create a `T`. Kotlin's `T()` gives `type parameter 'T' is not an expression.`, and Java's `new T()` gives `unexpected type`.
- A cast to a generic type checks only the class. This one compiles, with a warning, and it's the dangerous one:

```java
@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
List<String> lies = (List<String>) (Object) List.of(180, 150);
lies.size();                 // 2: the cast "worked"
String first = lies.get(0);  // ClassCastException: Integer cannot be cast to String
```

```kotlin
@Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST")
val lies = listOf(180, 150) as Any as List<String>
lies.size                    // 2: the cast "worked"
val first: String = lies[0]  // ClassCastException: Integer cannot be cast to String
```

`ErasureDemo` prints `the cast worked, size = 2`, then `ClassCastException at the read: class java.lang.Integer cannot be cast to class java.lang.String`. The cast worked. It just didn't check anything. The list now claims to hold names and holds weights, a state called **heap pollution**. The exception appears at the first read that needs a `String`, which may be in another class, written much later.

Some generic information does survive. The signatures of declarations (a field's type, a method's parameters, a class's superclass) stay in the class file, and reflection can read them: `Field.getGenericType()` on a `List<String>` field returns `java.util.List<java.lang.String>`. What erasure removes is the type argument of each object. Lesson 9 of this track puts the surviving part to work.

**A cast to a generic type checks only the class. Don't trust it to check the elements.**

So inside an ordinary generic function, `T` is gone. Kotlin has one way to bring it back.

aside.title: Why did Java choose erasure?
aside.body: Generics arrived in Java 5, in 2004, into a world full of compiled libraries that used raw `List` and `Map`. Erasure let a new `List<String>` and an old raw `List` be the same class at run time, so old and new code could call each other without being recompiled. The price is everything in this lesson. C# added generics a year later, in .NET 2.0, and chose the other way: its objects keep their type arguments at run time. Kotlin, compiling to the JVM, can't make that choice for objects. It can only bring the type back at the places where a function is called, which is the next section.

sections.h: A clerk who copies the label onto a note: inline and reified
sections.body:
Picture a second clerk at the door. This one knows the labels are about to come off. So before a label goes, the clerk copies it onto a note and pins the note to the job: "this job: apples". When the job reaches the shop floor, whoever does it can read the note.

Kotlin's version of that clerk has two parts. Mark a function **`inline`**, and the compiler doesn't build one shared body that every caller jumps to. It copies the function's body into each place that calls it. At each of those places, the type argument is known, because a call like `isA<Apple>()` is being compiled right there, with `Apple` in plain sight. Then mark the type parameter **`reified`**, from a word that means "made into a real thing". The compiler writes that real class into the copied body:

```java
// Java has no reified type parameters. The closest equivalent: pass the Class yourself.
static boolean isA(Object x, Class<?> type) { return type.isInstance(x); }

static <T> List<T> filterIsInstance(List<?> items, Class<T> type) {
    return items.stream().filter(type::isInstance).map(type::cast).toList();
}

isA(gala, Apple.class);                     // true
filterIsInstance(delivery, Apple.class);    // [Gala, Fuji]
```

```kotlin
inline fun <reified T> Any?.isA(): Boolean = this is T      // a real instanceof after inlining

gala.isA<Apple>()                           // true
delivery.filterIsInstance<Apple>()          // [Gala, Fuji]: the standard library's reified filter
```

`ReifiedDemo` sorts a mixed delivery of two apples, a lemon, a paper bag and a `null`, and prints `apples: [Gala, Fuji]` and `lemons: [Eureka]`. The figure shows what happened. After inlining, `gala.isA<Apple>()` isn't a call any more. In the caller's own bytecode, it has become `gala instanceof Apple`.

Inside a reified function, you get back what erasure took away: `x is T`, `x as T` and `x as? T` with a real check, plus `T::class` and `T::class.java`. The standard library relies on this for `filterIsInstance<T>()`, `emptyArray<T>()` and `typeOf<T>()`, which lesson 9 covers.

The rules follow from how it works:

| You write | Kotlin says |
|---|---|
| `fun <reified T> notInline(x: Any) = x is T` | `only type parameters of inline functions can be reified.` |
| `fun <T> forward(x: Any) = x.isA<T>()` | `cannot use 'T' as reified type parameter. Use a class instead.` |
| `classOf<Nothing>(TODO())` | `cannot use 'Nothing' as reified type parameter.` |

The first row is a clerk with no job to pin the note to. Without `inline` there is one shared body, compiled once for every caller, so there's nowhere to write the class. The second row matters most in practice. A reified function can only be called with a type the caller knows. If the caller is itself generic, with an ordinary `T`, its own label is already gone, so there is nothing to copy onto the note. The requirement spreads upward: the caller must be `inline` with a `reified T` too, or it must pass a real class.

**Inside an ordinary generic function, `T` is gone. Make the function `inline` and `T` `reified` when you need its class.**

Java has no such clerk. It has been passing the class by hand since Java 5.

sections.h: Java hands over the class itself: Class<T> tokens
sections.body:
Before reified, the standard answer was a **class token**: pass the `Class<T>` object as an argument, and let it do the run-time work that the erased `T` can't. Java never got the note, so it carries the label around by hand. Many Java libraries still look like this, such as a database library's `find(Apple.class, id)` or a text reader's `read(text, Apple.class)`. `type.isInstance(x)` is a checked `is T`, and `type.cast(x)` is a checked `as T`, with no warning. Kotlin writes the same token as `Apple::class.java`.

Good Kotlin libraries offer both. A core function takes a `Class<T>` (or a `KClass<T>`, Kotlin's own class object, which lesson 9 covers) and works for everyone. A one-line reified wrapper on top keeps Kotlin call sites short. `ClassTokenDemo` does that for the shop's standard items: ask for "an apple" without saying which, and you get a Gala:

```java
// Java calling the Kotlin functions in ClassTokenDemo.kt:
Apple apple = ClassTokenDemoKt.defaultOf(Apple.class);        // the Class-token core: fine
Apple viaReified = ClassTokenDemoKt.<Apple>defaultOf();       // error: method defaultOf ... cannot be applied to given types
```

```kotlin
fun <T : Any> defaultOf(type: Class<T>): T =
    type.cast(defaults[type] ?: throw IllegalArgumentException("no default for ${type.simpleName}"))

inline fun <reified T : Any> defaultOf(): T = defaultOf(T::class.java)

val apple: Apple = defaultOf()          // T inferred from the expected type
```

Both versions print `apple = Gala, lemon = Eureka, blank = ''`.

Why can't Java call the wrapper? javac can't inline Kotlin code, so it has no way to fill in `T`. Kotlin still writes a method for the wrapper into the class file, but marks it **synthetic**, a flag that means "made by the compiler, not for callers". The Java compiler ignores synthetic methods. Read the error again. javac says `defaultOf` needs an argument, because the only `defaultOf` it can see is the Class-token one. A reified function with no such overload gives `cannot find symbol`.

**If Java code will call your API, give it a `Class<T>` version. Make the reified one a one-line wrapper.**

One trap with tokens: `Int::class.java` is the primitive class `int`, but `T::class.java` for a reified `Int` is `java.lang.Integer`, the boxed class. A table filled with one and asked for the other finds nothing, and the Try-it's last step ends with `no default for Integer`. Use `Int::class.javaObjectType` when you need the boxed class. Java has the same split: `int.class` and `Integer.class` are different objects.

A class token and a reified `T` both carry a class. Neither one carries more than that.

sections.h: What the note can't hold: the limits of reified
sections.body:
Reified brings back the class at the call site, and only the class. The note has room for one word. Three limits are worth knowing.

First, the type arguments of `T` itself are still erased. `filterIsInstance<List<String>>()` compiles without a single warning, and it keeps every list:

```java
// the Java version passes List.class: there is no List<String>.class
List<List<String>> nameLists = filterIsInstance(boxes, List.class);
System.out.println(nameLists);                // [[180, 150], [Gala]]
String n = nameLists.get(0).get(0);           // ClassCastException
```

```kotlin
val boxes: List<Any> = listOf(listOf(180, 150), listOf("Gala"), "Fuji")
val nameLists = boxes.filterIsInstance<List<String>>()   // no warning
println(nameLists)                            // [[180, 150], [Gala]]
val n: String = nameLists[0][0]               // ClassCastException
```

The list of weights got through. The note said "List", and had no room for "of names". The Kotlin docs say the same about their own `asPairOf<String, List<String>>()` example: it "compiles but breaks type safety". After inlining, `is List<String>` is only `instanceof List`.

Second, `Nothing` and erased type parameters can't be reified, as the table in the second section showed.

Third, Kotlin 2.4 added an error about null. In `inline fun <reified T> klassOf(x: T) = x::class`, `T` may be a nullable type, so `x` may be `null`, and `null` has no class. Kotlin 2.3 warned about this, and 2.4 refuses: `expression in class literal has nullable type 'T (of fun <T> klassOf)'. Use '!!' to make the type non-nullable.` The fix is to say what you mean with `<reified T : Any>`, the bound from lesson 2 that keeps null out, so callers can't pass `null` at all. `T::class`, the class of the type rather than of a value, is still allowed with a nullable bound. Java has no such check: `x.getClass()` on a null `x` throws `NullPointerException` at run time, as `LimitsDemoJava` shows.

So treat reified as a tool for the outer class of a type: instance checks, casts and class tokens. When the full type matters, `List<Apple>` and not just `List`, you need something that keeps the type arguments. That's `KType`, in the next lesson.

java.title: Parsers.java

kotlin.title: Parsers.kt

compare.note: Both languages erase `T` inside `parse`, so both cores need the `Class<T>` argument, and both use `Class.cast` for a cast that really checks. The difference is at the call site. Kotlin can add an `inline` wrapper with a `reified T`, and the compiler fills in `Weight::class.java` for the caller. Java can't use that wrapper: it is a synthetic method in the class file, and javac can't inline it. Note also that the wrapper calls only public members. A public inline function is copied into other modules, so it may not touch `byType` directly (`public-API inline function cannot access non-public-API property`).

worked.title: Give a text reader a real type

steps.say: The shop reads its delivery notes with a text reader that, like many Java libraries, wants a class token: `fun <T : Any> read(text: String, type: Class<T>): T`. The first draft tries to hide the token behind a generic function. Read the error that names `T`.
steps.code:
fun <T : Any> load(text: String): T = reader.read(text, T::class.java)
// error: cannot use 'T' as reified type parameter. Use a class instead.
steps.alt_code:
static <T> T load(String text) { return reader.read(text, T.class); }
// error: cannot select from a type variable

steps.say: 1. Make the token explicit. This version works from Kotlin and from Java, and the reader does a checked conversion.
steps.code:
fun <T : Any> load(text: String, type: Class<T>): T = reader.read(text, type)

val a = load(text, Apple::class.java)
steps.alt_code:
static <T> T load(String text, Class<T> type) { return reader.read(text, type); }

Apple a = load(text, Apple.class);

steps.say: 2. Add the Kotlin convenience on top. Self-check before reading the comment: why must the wrapper be `inline`? (Only an inlined body is compiled at the call site, where `T` is known.)
steps.code:
inline fun <reified T : Any> load(text: String): T = load(text, T::class.java)

val a: Apple = load(text)          // T inferred from the expected type
val l = load<Lemon>(text)
steps.alt_code:
// Java can't call the reified wrapper; it keeps using the token version:
Lemon l = load(text, Lemon.class);

steps.say: 3. Check the limit before you rely on it. `load<List<Apple>>(text)` compiles, but it passes `List::class.java`. The reader has no element type to fill the list with (a JSON library such as Jackson fills it with maps), and the first `for (a: Apple in apples)` throws `ClassCastException`. For generic targets you need a token that keeps type arguments: `typeOf<List<Apple>>()` or a super type token, both in lesson 9.

drill.prompt: Close this page. Write `asOrNull<T>()` and `instancesOf<T>(items)` in Kotlin with reified type parameters. Then write the Java versions, which have to take a `Class<T>`. Which line in each Kotlin function would fail to compile, or quietly stop checking, without `reified`?

alt.title: Reified.java

recap: The JVM erases type arguments: at run time a `List<String>` is just a `List`, and `ArrayList<String>` and `ArrayList<Int>` share one class. The label comes off after the check.
So `is List<String>`, `is T` and `T()` don't compile, and a cast to `List<String>` checks only the class. The `ClassCastException` comes at a later read.
Declarations keep their generic signatures in the class file; objects keep none.
`inline` copies a function into each call site, and `reified` writes the caller's real class into the copy, so `is T`, `as? T` and `T::class` work.
Java can't call reified functions, because they are synthetic. Offer a `Class<T>` version, and make the reified one a one-line wrapper.
The limit: reified covers the outer class only, so `filterIsInstance<List<String>>()` keeps every list. In Kotlin 2.4, `x::class` on a nullable reified `T` is an error; use `T : Any`.
closing:
We started at the storeroom door, where the clerk checks each label and then tears it off. That's erasure: `List<Apple>` becomes `List`, a cast to a generic type checks only the class, and `is List<Int>` can't compile. An `inline` function with a `reified T` is the clerk who copies the label onto a note first, a note one word long. Java passes the class by hand instead.

Now search your code for `@Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST")` next to `as T` or `as List<`. Each one is a cast that checks nothing.

Next, we'll look closely at the class objects themselves. If a `Class` can only say `List`, what can keep the whole type `List<Apple>`?

quiz.q: `fun <T> isType(x: Any): Boolean = x is T`. What happens?
options: It compiles and checks against whatever `T` the caller used
It doesn't compile: `Cannot check for instance of erased type 'T'`
It compiles with a warning and always returns `true`
It compiles and throws at run time
quiz.why: Inside an ordinary generic function `T` is erased, so there is no class to check against. Kotlin refuses the check outright, instead of warning as it does for casts. Making the function `inline` with a `reified T` fixes it.

quiz.q: `@Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") val names = loadAny() as List<String>`, where `loadAny()` really returns `listOf(180, 150)`. Then `println(names.size)`, then `val first: String = names[0]`. Which line throws?
options: The cast
`println(names.size)`
`val first: String = names[0]`
None of them
quiz.why: The cast checks only that the object is a `List`, and `size` doesn't touch an element. The read is where the compiler inserted a cast to `String`, and that cast fails with `ClassCastException`. The bug is at the first line; the crash is at the third.

quiz.q: Java code in the same project will call your new Kotlin `parse` API. Which shape do you publish?
options: Only `inline fun <reified T : Any> parse(text: String): T`
`fun <T> parse(text: String): T` with an unchecked cast inside
A raw `Class` parameter, so any class works
`fun <T : Any> parse(text: String, type: Class<T>): T`, plus a one-line reified wrapper for Kotlin callers
quiz.why: javac can't call a reified function: it is a synthetic method, and Java can't inline it. A `Class<T>` core works for both languages and does a checked `type.cast`, and the reified wrapper keeps Kotlin call sites short. The unchecked cast checks nothing, and a raw `Class` loses the link between the argument and the return type.

options: `[[180], [Gala]]`: after inlining, the check is just `instanceof List`
`[[Gala]]`
A compile error: `List<String>` can't be a reified type argument
An unchecked-cast warning, then `[[Gala]]`
quiz.why: Reified fills in the outer class only, the one word on the note. The element type `String` is still erased, so both lists pass the check, and there isn't even a warning. Checking the elements yourself, or using a `KType`, is the only way to know more.

quiz.q: From "Star projection: when you don't know the type": `note: Any?` came from a file reader. Which code safely gets the `Int`s out of it?
options: `(note as List<Int>)`
`if (note is List<Int>) note else emptyList()`
`if (note is List<*>) note.filterIsInstance<Int>() else emptyList()`
`note as? List<Int> ?: emptyList()`
quiz.why: Check the shape with a star, then check each element: `filterIsInstance<Int>()` is reified on `Int`, a plain class, so each check is real. `is List<Int>` doesn't compile, and both casts check only that it's a list, so a stray `"bruised"` would blow up later.

flashcards.back: The compiler checks type arguments and then removes them. At run time a `List<String>` is just a `List`, with no record of `String`.

flashcards.front: Where does `val l = listOf(180) as Any as List<String>` fail?
flashcards.back: Not at the cast. It fails at the first read that needs a `String`, such as `val s: String = l[0]`.
`inline` copies the function body into each call site. `reified` writes the caller's real class for `T` into that copy, so `is T`, `as? T` and `T::class` work.

flashcards.front: Can Java call `inline fun <reified T : Any> parse(text: String): T`?
flashcards.back: No. It is a synthetic method, and javac can't inline it. Provide `parse(text, type: Class<T>)` as well.
No. Reified covers only the outer class; after inlining it is `instanceof List`, so a list of ints passes.

flashcards.front: Why is `inline fun <reified T> klassOf(x: T) = x::class` an error in Kotlin 2.4?
flashcards.back: `T` may be nullable, and `null` has no class. Write `<reified T : Any>`.
The first is the primitive `int`; the second is `java.lang.Integer`. Use `Int::class.javaObjectType` for the boxed class.

terms.plain: Removing type arguments after compile-time checking, so objects carry no `<String>` at run time.
A cast to a generic type that can check only the class. The compiler warns; the failure comes later.
A variable of a generic type that refers to an object of the wrong type, such as a `List<String>` holding ints.
A function whose body the compiler copies into each call site.
A type parameter of an inline function whose real class is available in the copied body.
A `Class<T>` passed as an argument, so code can check and cast to `T` at run time.
A method the compiler writes into the class file but hides from javac, as Kotlin does with reified functions.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate asks why `fun <T> load(text: String): T` can't just call `reader.read(text, T::class.java)`, but adding `inline` and `reified` makes it work. Explain it in your own words, and say what Java callers should use instead.
explain_back.answer: The JVM erases type arguments. An ordinary generic function has one compiled body, shared by every caller, and in that body `T` is just `Object`: nothing at run time says which `T` this call was for, so there is no class to hand to the reader. An `inline` function isn't called; its body is copied into each call site when that call site is compiled. At the call site the type argument is known, for example `load<Apple>(text)`. With `reified`, the compiler writes `Apple::class.java` into that copy, so the reader gets a real class. It's like copying the label onto a note before it's torn off. Java can't use this, because javac can't inline Kotlin code, and the reified function is a hidden synthetic method. Java callers need a version that takes a `Class<T>` explicitly, and the reified one should just call it. Even reified only gives the outer class: `load<List<Apple>>` would pass `List.class`.

deeper.body:
You can see the copy mechanism in the bytecode. Run `javap -c -p` on `ClassTokenDemoKt.class` (it is under `generics/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/generics/l08/demo/` after you run the demo). The method kept in the class for `defaultOf()` has the flags `ACC_PUBLIC, ACC_STATIC, ACC_FINAL, ACC_SYNTHETIC`, and where `T::class.java` should be, it loads `Object.class` next to a call to `kotlin/jvm/internal/Intrinsics.reifiedOperationMarker`. That marker tells the compiler where to write the real class when it copies the body into a caller. In `main`, the call `defaultOf<Lemon>()` has no call to `defaultOf()` at all: you'll find `ldc class workbench/generics/l08/demo/Lemon` followed by a call to the Class-token `defaultOf`.

This is also why the lab routes test calls through `Callers.kt`. The inlined copy is fixed when the caller is compiled. Tests compiled once against `src/main` would keep a copy of your TODO stub forever, even when run next to the reference solution.

Two more rules come from copying. A public inline function is copied into other modules, so it may only touch public API: reading a private field gives `public-API inline function cannot access non-public-API property`. That is the deep reason for the "Class-token core plus one-line reified wrapper" shape. And a lambda passed to an inline function is normally inlined too, so it can't be stored. If the function needs to keep it, say in a table of listeners, that parameter must be marked `noinline`. Lesson 11 of this track uses that for a typed event bus.

Java's own answer to erasure for arrays is different: arrays are reified. Every `String[]` knows its element type at run time, which is why `new T[1]` is a compile error (`generic array creation`), and why Kotlin's `arrayOf<T>()` needs a reified `T`.
